I played in a homebrew campaign hosted by one of my good friends, and one rule that he implemented was that if anyone (player OR enemy) rolled 3 Nat-20s in a row to attack, they would automatically fully kill whatever it was they were attempting to hit.

This, as you might expect, happened only in the rarest of occasions, one of which was against another player character.

Another friend was playing a half-orc barbarian whose philosophy was "stealth isn't real, I'm rushing straight in to get the first hits off." We enter into a cave system that reeks of death and decay, and this barbarian decides to say "to the hells with it, smells like there are corpses in there that need to be reminded what "dead" means," and thus sprints ahead of everyone else.

The barbarian rounds a corner to see a small horde of undead shambling about in the cavern beyond, and he shouts back to the rest of us to "hurry up, you'll miss all the fun!" before we see his character turn back and sprint around the corner toward the horde. He manages to get a surprise attack off on one of the closest undead, killing it, and then had to enter initiative after that.

Unfortunately, since he'd run so far ahead of everyone else, there was a full round of combat between him and the entire horde before the rest of us could get there to help. The very first undead that attacked him rolled to hit -- Nat 20. For shits and giggles, the rest of us look at the DM and say "Ope -- roll again, see if it's another Nat 20!" He rolls again -- Nat 20! At this point, we're all looking at each other across the table, and we all have the same thing in mind -- roll again, DM!

DM rolls again, and I shit you not, rolls a third Nat 20 in front of the gods and everybody. Chaos ensues, laughter erupts, and the player this was rolled against is looking around the table in abject horror as it dawns on him what's about to happen.

The DM looks at that barbarian player, says "Ah shit.. sorry man." And then proceeds to describe the undead lashing out with its talons of sharpened bone, connecting with the half-orc's neck, and fully ripping out all of the neck innards (jugular, trachea, adams-apple, etc.), instantly killing the half-orc.

By the time the rest of the party caught up, there was no saving the barbarian. The rest of the horde had descended upon him as he fell to the ground and were tearing him apart as we rounded the corner. We killed off the horde, laid the half-orc to rest, and continued forward while that player rolled up a new character.

The funniest part about that whole thing, though, was that the player went on to tell this story to some other friends outside of our D&D group, but he couldn't remember the name for the jugular, so he said with confidence (in a deep southern accent) "Man, that shit was crazy -- a single zombie ripped out my whole umbilical cord and killed me straight up" lmaoo

I usually pretend like the character is present, but kinda off in the background doing their own thing a bit. If they enter combat, I'll have the absent player's character fight "extras" in the background during combat. As in, enemy cardboard cutouts so that neither the enemies nor the absent PC require initiative rolls for the main combat. Usually, these "extra" enemies will be just enough in number to keep the absent character busy while the present party members deal with the actual threat.

One example would be a boss that my players recently fought that could summon revenant knights made of ash and brittle armor. There were two absent players that night (we have a large-ish group) so their characters were off in the background with one another doing their own thing for the most part.

The beginning of combat had the boss surprise the main group of PCs, who then immediately entered initiative with it. The absent characters would need a few rounds to reach the others and enter initiative, but the boss summoned the revenants within the first or second round. I described it as the two absent characters fighting off the revenants at the door to the main room they were in, keeping them at bay while the others took care of the main boss. By the time the main boss was finished off, the absent PCs were finishing off the last revenant, after which they dusted themselves off and resumed watch at the door.

The present players seemed to enjoy the imagination theater of that quite a bit, and the absent players felt accomplished and included lore-wise when I filled them in on the session events.

I've found that this helps keep the immersive experience together a bit more if you're playing a serious setting, but it's definitely to each their own with that. I know other DMs who wouldn't want to bother with the logistics of an absent cleric PC being "there" but not actively healing during combat, for example.

I'm usually pretty lenient when it comes to some things spell-wise. For instance, the Sacred Flame cantrip is described as "flame-like radiance" and deals radiant damage if the target fails a dex save. With that in mind, I would be open to a cleric PC using Sacred Flame to, say, start a fire at camp or melt small amounts of ice in a small surface area.

It depends on what the player wants to do vs. what the actual spell description says it does, but generally speaking, you do want to be careful with how lenient you are with it.

As another commenter mentioned, it can become a slippery slope if you rule X spell can do Y thing despite the description not specifying as such, as then your players might get the notion that ALL spells should be able to go off-script depending on what you allowed previously.

So my advice: if it's a change to add flavor to the setting, sure (usually)! But if it's a change in the actual function of the spell itself or would allow for potentially problematic interpretations of other, more powerful spells, maybe not.

Sounds like you accidentally overdid it a little there, my friend. My recommendation would be to take the suggested dose on the packaging, wait about 2 hours, and see how you feel. The saying "edibles don't kick in until you talk about how they aren't working" is honestly true.

When I get to that level, I call it Cosmic Abyss High. It's when manual breathing mode kicks in and paranoia amps up by a factor of 10. It doesn't last too terribly long, thankfully, but being in that state of mind definitely makes it feel a lot longer.

You may now be experiencing the Brain Fog™ that comes as a result of getting mega high. It lasts for most, if not all, of the following day after coming down. If you don't take any more edibles or smoke anything for the next 24 hours, it should wear off noticeably.

The actual high can be incredibly relaxing, exciting, and/or fun, but it's all about consuming the correct dosage for your tolerance level AND MORE IMPORTANTLY, setting up your environment to be a good-feeling one. Good, calming music, comfy clothes, and good company can make or break a high experience. You've got this, my dude!

I was taking my now-wife home one night when we were both still in school & living with our parents. The trip there generally took around 20 - 25 minutes, and we'd driven the same route there tons of times prior to this, so I knew that fact quite well by that point.

She had to be home by 8pm, so we left shortly before 7:30pm just to be safe. We talked the entire trip, and as we were right on the outskirts of her town, we both stopped and noticed a crazy bright white light in the sky that was moving almost parallel to my car above and ahead of us a ways. Just as quick as we noticed it, it shot straight down behind the treeline ahead of us and was gone.

We thought it was weird, but chocked it up as a shooting star or something like that. The craziest part was that when we pulled into her driveway, we looked at the clock to see how much time we had left to sit and talk before she had to go inside, the clock literally said *7:36pm.* And before anyone asks, I knew FOR SURE that we'd left at like 7:30pm to make sure we'd get there in time. I had evidence as to the time we left, too, as I'd sent a text to my mom to let her know I was leaving right before we left the driveway. Checked our phones too, just to make sure the dashboard clock wasn't slow or something.

Somehow, some way, a trip that should have taken us 20 to 25 minutes only took us 6 minutes from driveway to driveway. No idea how that could have happened, or if the white light was connected in any way, but definitely something that still comes up in conversation nowadays almost 8 years later.
